messages.subject: Confusing geom_bar call
parts:
> I'll start by talking about existing issues with mapping vs. setting
> aesthetics. One of the things that ggplot2 beginners have the hardest time
> with is the distinction between putting a variable inside of aes() as
> opposed to outside of it. I can understand the confusion -- I remember
> experiencing it myself at one point.
>
> Adding to the confusion is that variables that are set (outside of aes) get
> mixed in with other stuff. Here's an example:
>   geom_bar(aes(fill=var1), colour="black", position="dodge")
> In this case, 'colour' is similar to 'fill' in that it's an aesthetic, but
> syntax-wise, it's on a par with 'position', which is something else
> entirely. It does all makes some sense after you've been using it a while
> and internalize the concept of aesthetics and mappings, but at first this
> can be challenging.
>
> One possible solution is to make it so users have to be more explicit about
> what's mapped and what's set, as in:
>   geom_bar(aes(fill=var1), set(colour="black"), position="dodge")

I agree that geom_bar is currently quite confusing - it mixes
parameters for the layer, the geom and the stat (but not the
adjustment!). In the future, I'd like to geom_bar to refer
specifically to the geom (as it does in the layers package). There
it's quite clear what arguments geom_bar has:

geom_bar <- function(aesthetics = list(), na.rm = FALSE) {
...
}

i.e. a list of aesthetics and a parameter controlling what happens to missing.

So the first thing I'd like to do when clearing up the general
parameter confusion is to clear up the confusion between the geom and
the layer.

In the future, to add a "bar chart" layer to a plot, you'd use
layer_bar. I think this would look like:

layer_bar <- function(mapping, data, geom = "bar", stat = "identity",
adjust = "stack", inherit.aes = TRUE, show_guide = NA) {
..
}

which would be shortcut for

layer_bar <- function(mapping, data, geom = geom_bar(), stat =
stat_identity(), adjust = adjust_stack(), inherit.aes = TRUE,
show_guide = NA) {
..
}

The most explicit way of specifying (e.g.) blue bars would be:

layer_bar(geom = geom_bar(list(fill = "blue")))

The challenge is coming up with a short cut form that works in most
situations. One option would be to adapt what happens currently (but
with a better design for stats, geoms and adjusts this code would be
simpler and more flexible). For example, just focussing on the geom
part:

layer_bar <- function(geom = "bar", ...) {
args <- list()
if (is.character(geom)) {
geom <- match.fun(paste("geom", "bar", sep = "_"))
geom_args <- args[intersect(names(args), names(formals(geom)))]
geom <- geom(geom_args)
}
stopifnot(is.geom(geom))
...
}

So then you could do:

layer_bar(aesthetics = list(fill = "blue"))

I'm still thinking about the names of the arguments and their order,

> In other words, all mapped vars go in aes(), all the set variables go in
> set(), and other stuff goes outside. The trade-off for the added clarity is
> a little verbosity, but I think it's worth it -- I think it'll both be
> easier for beginners to understand, and force them to start thinking the
> right way.

What do you think of the approach I laid out above? I think it's
pretty similar to your ideas (if a little more concrete), and maybe it
just needs some tweaking of the parameter names.

> Moving on to "decoration"... These could be treated as aesthetics that can
> only be set; mapping variables to them is invalid. Conceptually speaking,
> decorations are aesthetic properties -- just ones that it doesn't make sense
> to map variables to. Here's an example where 'linejoin' is the decoration:
>   geom_bar (aes(fill=var1), set(colour="black", linejoin="round"))

Yes, so that corresponds exactly to the parameter of the geom. What
you're saying suggests is equivalent to saying the layers::geom_bar
should have linejoin argument.

> From a development point of view, one advantage of doing things this way is
> that you could implement something as a decoration at first, and then later
> you could promote it to a mappable aesthetic, without breaking existing user
> code. For example, maybe today I think that 'arrow' should be a decoration
> (can set, but not map), but for the next version of ggplot2, I decide that
> it should be a mappable aesthetic. It would be possible to add this
> capability without interfering with existing user code.

And I think you do get that with layer geoms. The only problem is
that the documentation currently doesn't specify what aesthetics a
geom can use, but the methods are all there to verify that correct
aesthetics are supplied.

> Overall, I think main the advantages to doing this way are conceptual
> clarity and syntactic consistency, and the drawback is slightly more verbose
> syntax.

Agreed.
